CC + i = a long "ch": RIC-CI = "reet-chee". CCH + i = a long "k": OC-CHI = "ok-kee".
Watch the double consonants: ca-PEL-li, bi-chi-CLET-ta. Hold them a little longer.
SC + a = "sk", as in Romanian: SKAP-PA-re. Not "sh"!
Review: GN = a soft "ny". Also in "bagnato" (wet), "sogno" (dream).
When you tell a story you use both tenses. Think of it as a film: the imperfetto is the set (what things were like, what was going on), the passato prossimo is the action that changes something.
The Romanian test: if in Romanian you'd say "era / făcea / cumpăram" → imperfetto. If you'd say "a fost / a făcut / am cumpărat" → passato prossimo. It works 90% of the time.
"Mentre" (while) almost always introduces an action in progress → imperfetto. "Quando" (when) usually introduces an event → passato prossimo.
While I was paying, I heard a noise.
When I arrived, Giulia was sleeping.
While I was cooking, Pietro was watching TV. (two parallel backgrounds)

An action limited in time takes the passato prossimo, even if it lasted a long time: "Ho abitato a Sibiu per vent'anni" (I lived there for 20 years — a closed period). But "Da piccolo abitavo a Sibiu" (description, no limit).
For build and character use ESSERE + adjective; for parts of the body, AVERE + noun + adjective:
È alto / basso / di statura media.
Ha i capelli biondi / castani / neri / grigi.
Ha i capelli ricci / lisci / mossi.
È calvo. È biondo. È bruno.
Ha gli occhi azzurri / verdi / castani.
Ha la barba / i baffi / un tatuaggio.
Clothes and accessories: PORTARE. "Porta gli occhiali" (he wears glasses), "portava una giacca verde" (he was wearing a green jacket).
"I capelli" is always plural: "Ha i capelli biondi" (he has blond hair). Not "il capello biondo" — that would be a single hair!
a young man / a young woman (up to about 30)
Useful phrases at the police (carabinieri, polizia) or for lost property:
I'd like to report a crime.
It happened last night at about nine.

When Matei brought the bike back, Graziella wasn't angry. She was thoughtful. "Sit down," she said. "Today is the 4th of November. Let me tell you a story."
"In 1966 I was twelve. That autumn it had been raining for weeks. On the evening of the 3rd of November the Arno was very high and brown, but nobody was afraid. Florence was used to rain.
At about four in the morning, while everyone was asleep, my father heard a strange noise. He went down into the trattoria: the water was already coming in under the door.
He woke us up and we all went up to the second floor, to the room where you sleep now. From the window I could see the street turning into a river. Cars, chairs, trees went past, even a cow.
My mother cried quietly. My father watched the water and said nothing. The trattoria was their life.
The next day the water went down and left a black, stinking mud everywhere, a metre deep. We lost everything: the tables, the chairs, the oven, my grandparents' photos.

But after a few days the young people came. They came from all over Italy and all over the world: students, young workers, foreigners. They called them 'the mud angels'. They cleaned the streets, the houses, the churches, and above all they saved the books and the paintings.

One afternoon a young man from Bologna came into the trattoria. He was tall, very thin, with curly black hair and a pair of broken glasses tied up with string. He wore huge boots and a jumper covered in mud. He was always laughing.
He worked with us for two weeks. Every evening my mother made him a hot soup. I was twelve and I looked at him like a hero.
Then he went back to Bologna. Nine years later, one spring Sunday, he walked into the trattoria again. He still had his curly hair and his glasses. His name was Aldo."
Graziella smiled and looked at the wedding photo on the wall. Matei said nothing. Only now did he understand why the grandmother was so fond of that old red bicycle: it was Aldo's.
